docs.title: 🧩 Sliding Window
docs.text:
Use for contiguous subarray / substring problems driven by sums, counts, or uniqueness.

Template (variable size): 

def longest_substring_no_repeat(s: str) -> int:
  last = {}
  left = 0
  best = 0
  for right, ch in enumerate(s):
    if ch in last and last[ch] >= left:
      left = last[ch] + 1  # shrink past last occurrence
    last[ch] = right
    best = max(best, right - left + 1)
  return best
Pitfalls: forgetting to shrink window correctly when invariant breaks.

docs.title: 🪜 Two Pointers
docs.text:
Array / string traversal from both ends or with fast/slow for merging, dedupe, partition.

Template (sorted pair sum): 

def two_sum_sorted(a, target):
  i, j = 0, len(a) - 1
  while i < j:
    s = a[i] + a[j]
    if s == target:
      return i, j
    if s < target:
      i += 1
    else:
      j -= 1
  return None
Pitfall: infinite loop if indices not advanced on all branches.

docs.title: 🧮 Prefix / Difference Arrays
docs.text:
Range queries, subarray sums, balancing parentheses, difference updates.

Prefix sum template: 

ps = [0]
for x in arr:
  ps.append(ps[-1] + x)
# sum i..j = ps[j+1] - ps[i]
Pitfall: off-by-one indices.

docs.title: 🧵 Hash Map (Frequency / Index Maps)
docs.text:
Counting, first occurrence, sliding window uniqueness.

Two sum variant: 

def two_sum(nums, target):
  pos = {}
  for i, x in enumerate(nums):
    if target - x in pos:
      return pos[target - x], i
    pos[x] = i
Pitfall: storing duplicates incorrectly (need earliest vs latest index depending on problem).

docs.title: 🔗 Stack Patterns
docs.text:
Monotonic stack (next greater, largest rectangle), parentheses validation, evaluation.

Monotonic increasing example: 

def next_greater(nums):
  st = []
  ans = [-1] * len(nums)
  for i, x in enumerate(nums):
    while st and nums[st[-1]] < x:
      ans[st.pop()] = x
    st.append(i)
  return ans
Pitfall: forgetting to pop equals when required by spec.

docs.title: 🧬 Recursion & Backtracking
docs.text:
Permutations, combinations, subsets, N-Queens, partitioning.

Template: 

def backtrack(path, start):
  out.append(path[:])
  for i in range(start, len(nums)):
    path.append(nums[i])
    backtrack(path, i + 1)
    path.pop()
Pitfall: forgetting to undo state (path.pop()).

docs.title: 🧮 Binary Search on Answer
docs.text:
Search feasible minimal / maximal value (capacity, time, threshold).

Template: 

def binary_search_answer(lo, hi, feasible):
  while lo < hi:
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    if feasible(mid):
      hi = mid
    else:
      lo = mid + 1
  return lo
Pitfall: infinite loop with (lo+hi)//2 when lo+1==hi; ensure termination.

docs.title: 🧊 Dynamic Programming (1-D & 2-D)
docs.text:
State definition, transitions, base cases, order, space optimization.

Knapsack 0/1 (space optimized): 

def knapsack(W, wt, val):
  dp = [0] * (W + 1)
  for i, w in enumerate(wt):
    for c in range(W, w - 1, -1):
      dp[c] = max(dp[c], dp[c - w] + val[i])
  return dp[W]
Pitfall: iterating capacity forward ruins reuse of previous row.

docs.title: 🧪 Probabilistic / Randomized
docs.text:
Reservoir sampling, randomized quickselect, hashing for equality.

Reservoir sample k=1: 

import random

def reservoir(stream):
  pick = None
  for i, x in enumerate(stream, 1):
    if random.randrange(i) == 0:
      pick = x
  return pick

docs.title: Approach (greedy by “skip cost”)
docs.text:
• Let a = dispatch1 (you), b = dispatch2 (co-worker).
  • For each warehouse with inventory v, only v % (a+b) matters:
    • r = 0 ⇒ it empties on co-worker’s turn; to flip it to you requires consecutive extra moves from you. Minimal required skips = ceil(b/a).
    • 1 ≤ r ≤ a ⇒ already ends on your turn; +1 credit, 0 skips.
    • a < r < a+b ⇒ needs ceil(r/a) - 1 co-worker skips to make the final empty happen on your turn.
  • Collect all positive “skip costs”, sort ascending, spend the limited skips on the cheapest warehouses; each fully paid cost yields +1 credit.
  • Time: O(n log n) (sort of costs). Use 64-bit.
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

long long getMaximumCredits(const vector<long long>& inventory,
                            long long dispatch1, long long dispatch2,
                            long long skips) {
    long long a = dispatch1, b = dispatch2, ab = a + b;
    long long res = 0;
    vector<long long> cost;
    cost.reserve(inventory.size());

    for (long long v : inventory) {
        long long r = v % ab;
        if (r == 0) {
            cost.push_back((b + a - 1) / a);
        } else if (r <= a) {
            ++res;
        } else {
            cost.push_back((r + a - 1) / a - 1);
        }
    }

    sort(cost.begin(), cost.end());
    for (long long c : cost) {
        if (skips < c) break;
        skips -= c;
        ++res;
    }
    return res;
}

docs.title: Approach (DP over prefix-equality)
docs.text:
• Let s = primaryCode (length up to 1e5), t = backupCode (≤100).
  • Maintain:
    • equal[k]: #subsequences of s seen so far equal to t[0..k-1]. equal[0]=1 for empty subsequence.
    • gt: #subsequences already lexicographically greater than t.
  • For each char c in s:
    • Existing gt subsequences can either take or skip c: gt = 2*gt.
    • Any subsequence equal to t entirely (equal[m]) and taking c becomes lex-greater (since t is a prefix of a longer string): add equal[m].
    • For every k where c > t[k], taking c after a subsequence equal to t[0..k-1] becomes lex-greater: add sum(equal[k]) over such k.
    • Update equal for matches (c == t[k]) in reverse k to extend equals.
  • Modulo 1e9+7. Time O(|s| * |t|); space O(|t|).
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int findValidCredentials(const string& primaryCode, const string& backupCode) {
    const long long MOD = 1'000'000'007LL;
    int m = (int)backupCode.size();
    vector<long long> equal(m + 1, 0);
    equal[0] = 1;
    long long gt = 0;

    for (char c : primaryCode) {
        long long add = equal[m] % MOD;
        for (int k = 0; k < m; ++k)
            if (c > backupCode[k]) add = (add + equal[k]) % MOD;

        gt = (gt * 2 + add) % MOD;

        auto nxt = equal;
        for (int k = m - 1; k >= 0; --k)
            if (c == backupCode[k]) {
                nxt[k + 1] += equal[k];
                if (nxt[k + 1] >= MOD) nxt[k + 1] -= MOD;
            }
        equal.swap(nxt);
    }
    return (int)(gt % MOD);
}

docs.title: 📝 Description
docs.text: You are given a list of logical circuit expressions. Each expression is written in prefix notation using only logical operators and constants. You must evaluate each expression and return its result as either 1 (logical true) or 0 (logical false).

docs.title: 🔣 Supported Symbols
docs.text:
Symbol Meaning [ Start of expression block ] End of expression block & Logical AND | Logical OR ! Logical NOT 1 Logical TRUE 0 Logical FALSE

Each expression may be deeply nested and will follow correct prefix notation using the brackets [ and ] to group expressions.

docs.title: 🔁 Function Signature
docs.text: vector<int> circuitsOutput(vector<string> circuitsExpression);

docs.title: 📥 Input
docs.text:
• circuitsExpression: A list of strings, where each string is a valid circuit expression.
  • Each expression may contain up to 10^6 characters.

docs.title: 📤 Output
docs.text: • Return a list of integers where each value is either 1 or 0, representing the result of evaluating each expression.

docs.title: 🔒 Constraints
docs.text:
• 1 ≤ circuitsExpression.size() ≤ 10
  • Each expression is syntactically valid.
  • Only symbols: 0, 1, [, ], &, |, !, and commas (,) for separation.

docs.title: Output
docs.text: [1]

docs.title: ✅ C++ Solution
docs.text:
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int eval(queue<string> &q) {
    string t = q.front(); q.pop();
    if (t == "[") {
        string op = q.front(); q.pop();
        vector<int> args;
        while (q.front() != "]") {
            if (q.front() == "[") args.push_back(eval(q));
            else {
                string x = q.front(); q.pop();
                if (x == "!") {
                    int v = (q.front() == "[") ? eval(q) : (q.pop(), q.front() == "1");
                    if (q.front() != "[") q.pop();
                    args.push_back(!v);
                } else args.push_back(x == "1");
            }
        }
        q.pop(); // pop "]"
        if (op == "&") return all_of(args.begin(), args.end(), [](int x){ return x; });
        if (op == "|") return any_of(args.begin(), args.end(), [](int x){ return x; });
        if (op == "!") return !args[0];
    }
    return t == "1";
}

vector<int> circuitsOutput(vector<string> exprs) {
    vector<int> out;
    for (auto &s : exprs) {
        queue<string> q;
        for (size_t i = 0; i < s.size(); ++i) {
            if (isspace(s[i]) || s[i] == ',') continue;
            q.push(string(1, s[i]));
        }
        out.push_back(eval(q));
    }
    return out;
}

int main() {
    vector<string> expressions = {
        "[&, [&, 1, [!, 0]], [|, [|, 1, 0], [!, 1]]]"
    };
    vector<int> results = circuitsOutput(expressions);
    for (int res : results) cout << res << endl;  // Output: 1
}

docs.title: 📝 Description
docs.text: Given an array of non-negative integers, perform a series of operations until the array becomes empty. The score is updated at each operation based on the sum of elements currently in the array. The goal is to maximize the overall score at the end.

docs.title: 🔢 Operations
docs.text:
• Operations are 1-indexed.
  • Odd-indexed operation: Add the sum of all integers in the array to the score.
  • Even-indexed operation: Subtract the sum of all integers in the array from the score.
  • After each operation, you must remove either the leftmost or rightmost element to continue.

Return the maximum score possible.

docs.title: 📥 Input
docs.text:
• An array of integers integerArray with size n (1 ≤ n ≤ 1000)
  • Each element is in range 0 ≤ integerArray[i] ≤ 10⁹

docs.title: 📤 Output
docs.text: • Return an integer: the maximum possible score

docs.title: 📘 Example
docs.text:
Input 

integerArray = [1, 2, 3, 4, 2, 6]

Output 

13

Explanation

  • Op 1 (odd): score += 18 → score = 18 → remove 6 → arr = [1,2,3,4,2]
  • Op 2 (even): score -= 12 → score = 6 → remove 2 → arr = [1,2,3,4]
  • Op 3 (odd): score += 10 → score = 16 → remove 4 → arr = [1,2,3]
  • Op 4 (even): score -= 6 → score = 10 → remove 1 → arr = [2,3]
  • Op 5 (odd): score += 5 → score = 15 → remove 3 → arr = [2]
  • Op 6 (even): score -= 2 → score = 13 → arr = []

docs.title: ✅ C++ Solution
docs.text:
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

long long dp[1001][1001][2];

long long solve(const vector<int>& arr, int l, int r, int opIndex) {
    if (l > r) return 0;
    int parity = opIndex % 2;
    if (dp[l][r][parity] != LLONG_MIN) return dp[l][r][parity];

    long long total = accumulate(arr.begin() + l, arr.begin() + r + 1, 0LL);
    long long gain = (parity == 1) ? total : -total;

    long long removeLeft = gain + solve(arr, l + 1, r, opIndex + 1);
    long long removeRight = gain + solve(arr, l, r - 1, opIndex + 1);

    return dp[l][r][parity] = max(removeLeft, removeRight);
}

long long getMaximumScore(vector<int> integerArray) {
    int n = integerArray.size();
    for (int i = 0; i <= n; ++i)
        for (int j = 0; j <= n; ++j)
            dp[i][j][0] = dp[i][j][1] = LLONG_MIN;

    return solve(integerArray, 0, n - 1, 1);
}

int main() {
    vector<int> arr = {1, 2, 3, 4, 2, 6};
    cout << getMaximumScore(arr) << endl; // Output: 13

    // Example with large numbers to test overflow handling
    vector<int> bigArr(1000, 1000000000);
    cout << getMaximumScore(bigArr) << endl; // Should not overflow
}

docs.title: Flexport Interview DSA Questions (1–10) — Problems, Solutions & Explanations
1. Push Dominoes
docs.text:
Problem: Given a string of 'L', 'R', and '.', simulate the effect of domino pushes. Approach: Two passes — left-to-right to calculate rightward forces, right-to-left for leftward forces, compare to decide final state. Solution: 

def pushDominoes(s):
    n = len(s); L = [0]*n; R = [0]*n
    force = 0
    for i,c in enumerate(s):
        force = 0 if c=='L' else (n if c=='R' else max(force-1,0))
        R[i] = force
    force = 0
    for i in range(n-1,-1,-1):
        c = s[i]
        force = 0 if c=='R' else (n if c=='L' else max(force-1,0))
        L[i] = force
    ans=[]
    for i in range(n):
        if R[i]==L[i]: ans.append('.')
        elif R[i]>L[i]: ans.append('R')
        else: ans.append('L')
    return ''.join(ans)
Complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space.

docs.title: 2. Hex-string Two Sum
docs.text:
Problem: Given array of hex-string numbers and a hex target, return indices of two that sum to target. Approach: Convert to int, use hashmap for complement lookup. Solution: 

def two_sum_hex(nums, target_hex):
    target = int(target_hex, 16)
    seen = {}
    for i,xh in enumerate(nums):
        x = int(xh, 16)
        if target - x in seen:
            return [seen[target-x], i]
        seen[x] = i
Complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space.

docs.title: 3. Directed Graph Traversal / Cycle Detection
docs.text:
Problem: Given directed edges, detect cycles. Approach: DFS with 3-color marking. Solution: 

def has_cycle(n, edges):
    g = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u,v in edges: g[u].append(v)
    color = [0]*n
    def dfs(u):
        color[u]=1
        for v in g[u]:
            if color[v]==1: return True
            if color[v]==0 and dfs(v): return True
        color[u]=2; return False
    return any(dfs(u) for u in range(n) if color[u]==0)
Complexity: O(n+m).

docs.title: 4. Validate IP Address
docs.text:
Problem: Given a string, classify as IPv4, IPv6, or Neither. Approach: Split and validate by rules for each IP type. Solution: 

def validIPAddress(q):
    import string
    hexd = set(string.hexdigits)
    def v4(s):
        parts = s.split('.')
        if len(parts)!=4: return False
        for p in parts:
            if not p or (len(p)>1 and p[0]=='0'): return False
            if not p.isdigit(): return False
            x = int(p)
            if x<0 or x>255: return False
        return True
    def v6(s):
        parts = s.split(':')
        if len(parts)!=8: return False
        for p in parts:
            if not (1<=len(p)<=4): return False
            if not all(c in hexd for c in p): return False
        return True
    return "IPv4" if v4(q) else ("IPv6" if v6(q) else "Neither")
Complexity: O(len(s)).

docs.title: 5. Letter Combinations of a Phone Number
docs.text:
Problem: Map digit string to all possible letter combinations. Approach: Iterative expansion. Solution: 

def letterCombinations(digits):
    if not digits: return []
    M = {'2':'abc','3':'def','4':'ghi','5':'jkl','6':'mno','7':'pqrs','8':'tuv','9':'wxyz'}
    ans=['']
    for d in digits:
        ans = [p+c for p in ans for c in M[d]]
    return ans
Complexity: O(∏ choices).

docs.title: 6. Tile Removal Game
docs.text:
Problem: Remove contiguous runs of ≥3 identical tiles repeatedly. Approach: Stack to track character and count, remove when count ≥3. Solution: 

def crush(s):
    st=[]
    for ch in s:
        if st and st[-1][0]==ch:
            st[-1][1]+=1
            if st[-1][1]>=3:
                st.pop()
        else:
            st.append([ch,1])
    return ''.join(ch*cnt for ch,cnt in st)
Complexity: O(n).

docs.title: 7. Token–Card Purchase Logic
docs.text:
Problem: Determine if a player can buy a card given tokens, wildcards, and bonuses. Approach: Calculate deficits after bonuses, use wildcards if needed. Solution: 

def can_buy(tokens, wild, cost, bonus):
    deficit = 0
    pay = {}
    for c in cost:
        need = max(0, cost[c] - bonus.get(c,0))
        use = min(tokens.get(c,0), need)
        pay[c]=use
        deficit += (need - use)
    return (deficit <= wild), pay, wild - deficit
Complexity: O(colors).

docs.title: 8. Reservation System
docs.text:
Problem: Book non-overlapping intervals for each resource. Approach: Maintain sorted list per resource, binary search for placement. Solution: 

import bisect
class Scheduler:
    def __init__(self): self.map={}
    def book(self, rid, start, end):
        A = self.map.setdefault(rid, [])
        i = bisect.bisect_left(A, (start,end))
        if i>0 and A[i-1][1] > start: return False
        if i<len(A) and A[i][0] < end: return False
        A.insert(i,(start,end)); return True
Complexity: O(log n) search.

docs.title: 9. Connect Four (Infinite Board)
docs.text:
Problem: Place a piece and detect if player wins (4 in a row). Approach: Count in 4 directions from placed position. Solution: 

dirs=[(1,0),(0,1),(1,1),(1,-1)]
def win(board, r,c,p):
    def count(dr,dc):
        k=0; rr,cc=r+dr,c+dc
        while (rr,cc) in board and board[(rr,cc)]==p:
            k+=1; rr+=dr; cc+=dc
        return k
    for dr,dc in dirs:
        if 1+count(dr,dc)+count(-dr,-dc) >= 4:
            return True
    return False
Complexity: O(1) per move.

docs.title: 10. Checkers (Core Move Logic)
docs.text:
Problem: Generate legal moves in checkers, prioritizing captures. Approach: DFS for capture chains, normal moves if no captures. Solution (outline): 

def gen_moves(board, player):
    captures = []
    normals = []
    for p in all_pieces(board, player):
        caps = find_captures(board, p)
        if caps: captures += caps
        else: normals += find_steps(board, p)
    return captures if captures else normals
Complexity: Depends on branching factor, small in practice.

docs.title: 11. Median-Finding
docs.text:
Problem: Find the median from a stream of numbers. Approach: Use two heaps — max-heap for lower half, min-heap for upper half — to balance elements. Solution: 

import heapq
class MedianFinder:
    def __init__(self):
        self.low, self.high = [], []  # max-heap (invert sign) and min-heap
    def addNum(self, num):
        heapq.heappush(self.low, -num)
        heapq.heappush(self.high, -heapq.heappop(self.low))
        if len(self.low) < len(self.high):
            heapq.heappush(self.low, -heapq.heappop(self.high))
    def findMedian(self):
        if len(self.low) > len(self.high):
            return -self.low[0]
        return (-self.low[0] + self.high[0]) / 2
Complexity: O(log n) insert, O(1) median retrieval.

docs.title: 12. Implement a Sorting Algorithm
docs.text:
Problem: Implement quicksort from scratch. Approach: Choose pivot, partition, recursively sort halves. Solution: 

def quicksort(a):
    if len(a) <= 1: 
        return a
    pivot = a[len(a)//2]
    left = [x for x in a if x < pivot]
    mid  = [x for x in a if x == pivot]
    right = [x for x in a if x > pivot]
    return quicksort(left) + mid + quicksort(right)
Complexity: O(n log n) average, O(n^2) worst-case.

docs.title: 13. Graph Traversal Implementation
docs.text:
Problem: Traverse graph using BFS. Approach: Use queue to process nodes level by level. Solution: 

from collections import deque
def bfs(graph, start):
    vis = set([start])
    q = deque([start])
    order = []
    while q:
        u = q.popleft()
        order.append(u)
        for v in graph[u]:
            if v not in vis:
                vis.add(v)
                q.append(v)
    return order
Complexity: O(V+E).

docs.title: 14. Bug Hunt (Code Debugging)
docs.text: Problem: Given faulty code, identify and fix logical errors. Approach: Understand requirements, trace with test cases, fix incorrect conditions or loops. Note: Solution depends on specific buggy code — generally involves adding debug prints, verifying variables.

docs.title: 15. Binary Search on Answer
docs.text:
Problem: Given weights and days, find minimal ship capacity to deliver in D days. Approach: Binary search between max(weights) and sum(weights); greedily check feasibility. Solution: 

def shipWithinDays(weights, D):
    lo, hi = max(weights), sum(weights)
    def can(cap):
        days, total = 1, 0
        for w in weights:
            if total + w > cap:
                days += 1
                total = 0
            total += w
        return days <= D
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo+hi)//2
        if can(mid):
            hi = mid
        else:
            lo = mid+1
    return lo
Complexity: O(n log(sum-max)).

docs.title: 16. Dynamic Programming – Coin Change
docs.text:
Problem: Find the fewest coins needed to make a target amount. Approach: Bottom-up DP tracking minimal coins for each total. Solution: 

def coinChange(coins, amount):
    dp = [float('inf')] * (amount+1)
    dp[0] = 0
    for i in range(1, amount+1):
        for c in coins:
            if i-c >= 0:
                dp[i] = min(dp[i], dp[i-c]+1)
    return dp[amount] if dp[amount] != float('inf') else -1
Complexity: O(amount * len(coins)).

docs.title: 17. Graph: DFS Basics
docs.text:
Problem: Perform a depth-first search on a graph. Approach: Use recursion or explicit stack to visit nodes. Solution: 

def dfs(graph, start, visited=None):
    if visited is None:
        visited = set()
    visited.add(start)
    for v in graph[start]:
        if v not in visited:
            dfs(graph, v, visited)
    return visited
Complexity: O(V+E).

docs.title: 18. Multi-Stage Problem + OOP Extensions
docs.text:
Problem: Solve an algorithm problem, then wrap in a class with clean API. Approach: Start procedural, refactor into OOP for extensibility. Example: 

class Sorter:
    def sort(self, arr):
        return sorted(arr)

docs.title: 20. Permission or Simulation Logic
docs.text:
Problem: Simulate a system with state transitions based on actions. Approach: Map states to allowed transitions; iterate through action sequence. Solution: 

def simulate(actions, rules, start_state):
    state = start_state
    for act in actions:
        if act in rules[state]:
            state = rules[state][act]
        else:
            return False
    return True
Complexity: O(len(actions)).

docs.title: 21. Merge K Sorted Lists
docs.text:
Problem: Merge k sorted linked lists into one sorted list. Approach: Use a min-heap to repeatedly extract the smallest head node. Solution: 

import heapq
def mergeKLists(lists):
    heap = []
    for i, node in enumerate(lists):
        if node:
            heapq.heappush(heap, (node.val, i, node))
    dummy = curr = ListNode(0)
    while heap:
        val, i, node = heapq.heappop(heap)
        curr.next = node
        curr = curr.next
        if node.next:
            heapq.heappush(heap, (node.next.val, i, node.next))
    return dummy.next
Complexity: O(N log k), where N is total nodes.

docs.title: 22. Sliding Window — Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
docs.text:
Problem: Given a string, find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters. Approach: Use a sliding window with a hashmap to track indices. Solution: 

def lengthOfLongestSubstring(s):
    seen = {}
    left = max_len = 0
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        if ch in seen and seen[ch] >= left:
            left = seen[ch] + 1
        seen[ch] = right
        max_len = max(max_len, right - left + 1)
    return max_len
Complexity: O(n) time, O(k) space.

docs.title: 23. Monotonic Stack — Largest Rectangle in Histogram
docs.text:
Problem: Find largest rectangle area in histogram bars. Approach: Use stack to maintain increasing bar heights. Solution: 

def largestRectangleArea(heights):
    stack = []
    max_area = 0
    heights.append(0)
    for i, h in enumerate(heights):
        while stack and heights[stack[-1]] > h:
            height = heights[stack.pop()]
            width = i if not stack else i - stack[-1] - 1
            max_area = max(max_area, height * width)
        stack.append(i)
    return max_area
Complexity: O(n).

docs.title: 24. Union-Find — Connected Components
docs.text:
Problem: Given n nodes and edges, count connected components. Approach: Union-Find data structure. Solution: 

def countComponents(n, edges):
    parent = list(range(n))
    def find(x):
        while x != parent[x]:
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]
            x = parent[x]
        return x
    def union(a, b):
        ra, rb = find(a), find(b)
        if ra != rb:
            parent[ra] = rb
    for u, v in edges:
        union(u, v)
    return len({find(i) for i in range(n)})
Complexity: O(α(n)) amortized.

docs.title: 25. Trie — Autocomplete
docs.text:
Problem: Implement a trie with insert and search (prefix match). Approach: Each node stores children and end-of-word flag. Solution: 

class TrieNode:
    def __init__(self):
        self.children = {}
        self.is_end = False

class Trie:
    def __init__(self):
        self.root = TrieNode()
    def insert(self, word):
        node = self.root
        for ch in word:
            if ch not in node.children:
                node.children[ch] = TrieNode()
            node = node.children[ch]
        node.is_end = True
    def search(self, word):
        node = self.root
        for ch in word:
            if ch not in node.children:
                return False
            node = node.children[ch]
        return node.is_end
    def startsWith(self, prefix):
        node = self.root
        for ch in prefix:
            if ch not in node.children:
                return False
            node = node.children[ch]
        return True
Complexity: O(L) per op, where L is word length.

docs.title: 26. Interval Merge
docs.text:
Problem: Merge overlapping intervals. Approach: Sort by start, merge into output list. Solution: 

def merge(intervals):
    intervals.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])
    merged = []
    for start, end in intervals:
        if not merged or merged[-1][1] < start:
            merged.append([start, end])
        else:
            merged[-1][1] = max(merged[-1][1], end)
    return merged
Complexity: O(n log n).

docs.title: 27. Grid DP — Unique Paths
docs.text:
Problem: Find unique paths from top-left to bottom-right in m×n grid. Approach: DP table where dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1]. Solution: 

def uniquePaths(m, n):
    dp = [[1]*n for _ in range(m)]
    for i in range(1, m):
        for j in range(1, n):
            dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1]
    return dp[-1][-1]
Complexity: O(mn).

docs.title: 28. Longest Increasing Subsequence (n log n)
docs.text:
Problem: Find LIS length. Approach: Patience sorting using binary search. Solution: 

import bisect
def lengthOfLIS(nums):
    sub = []
    for x in nums:
        i = bisect.bisect_left(sub, x)
        if i == len(sub):
            sub.append(x)
        else:
            sub[i] = x
    return len(sub)
Complexity: O(n log n).

docs.title: 29. Topological Sort — Course Schedule
docs.text:
Problem: Given prerequisites, find if all courses can be finished. Approach: Kahn's algorithm (BFS on in-degree). Solution: 

from collections import deque
def canFinish(numCourses, prerequisites):
    g = [[] for _ in range(numCourses)]
    indeg = [0]*numCourses
    for u,v in prerequisites:
        g[v].append(u)
        indeg[u]+=1
    q = deque([i for i in range(numCourses) if indeg[i]==0])
    visited = 0
    while q:
        u = q.popleft()
        visited+=1
        for v in g[u]:
            indeg[v]-=1
            if indeg[v]==0:
                q.append(v)
    return visited == numCourses
Complexity: O(V+E).

docs.title: 30. BFS/DFS on Grid — Number of Islands
docs.text:
Problem: Count islands in a binary grid. Approach: DFS or BFS flood-fill from each unvisited '1'. Solution: 

def numIslands(grid):
    if not grid: return 0
    m, n = len(grid), len(grid[0])
    def dfs(i, j):
        if i<0 or i>=m or j<0 or j>=n or grid[i][j] != '1':
            return
        grid[i][j] = '0'
        for di, dj in [(1,0),(-1,0),(0,1),(0,-1)]:
            dfs(i+di, j+dj)
    count = 0
    for i in range(m):
        for j in range(n):
            if grid[i][j] == '1':
                dfs(i, j)
                count += 1
    return count
Complexity: O(mn).

docs.title: Flexport SDE‑2 — High‑Level Design (HLD) Master Pack
docs.text:
A practical, interview‑ready playbook with detailed solutions for 15 systems. Each section gives you: requirements, API, data model, reference architecture, consistency strategy, scaling plan, failure modes, security/PII, and “talk track” bullets.

Tip: In the interview, spend ~3–5 min on requirements, 5–8 min on architecture, 5–7 min on data/consistency, 3–5 min on scaling+ops, and finish with trade‑offs & evolution.

docs.title: 1) Global Shipment Tracking Platform
docs.text: Ingest carrier/webhook/EDI events; dedupe; handle out‑of‑order; project “current status” and serve timelines.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Functional: ingestEvent, getCurrentStatus(shipmentId), getTimeline(shipmentId), search(shipper, lane, time).
  • SLOs: P99 ingest < 200 ms; query P99 < 100 ms for hot shipments.
  • Scale: 10–50k events/min; 10M shipments active; retention 2 years.
  • Constraints: out‑of‑order events; duplicate sources; multi‑tenant.

docs.title: API (sketch)
docs.text:
POST /v1/events {idemKey, shipmentId, legId?, containerId?, type, ts, location, payload}
GET  /v1/shipments/{id}/status
GET  /v1/shipments/{id}/timeline?limit&cursor
GET  /v1/shipments/search?shipperId&port&since&until&page&size

docs.title: Data Model
docs.text:
• events(shipment_id, event_id, ts, type, source, leg_id, container_id, location, payload_json, idem_key UNIQUE, created_at)
  • shipment_projection(shipment_id PK, status, last_ts, last_location, last_leg_id, version)
  • leg_projection(leg_id PK, shipment_id, from_port, to_port, planned_etd, planned_eta, actual_departed_at, actual_arrived_at, status)
  • Index: (shipment_id, ts), (port, ts), (last_ts DESC).

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
• Ingress: API → Kafka topic shipment-events.
  • Dedup: idemKey check (Redis BF + DB UNIQUE).
  • Projectors (CQRS): consume events → update projections (optimistic CAS on version).
  • Reads: API → Redis cache (hot) → projections DB; timelines from events store (append‑only).
  • Storage: events in BigTable/Scylla/Timescale; projections in Postgres; cache in Redis.
Sources -> API -> Kafka -> Projector(s) -> Projections DB
                               |--> Alerts/SLA Engine
Reads -> API -> Redis -> Projections DB / Events Store

docs.title: Consistency & Ordering
docs.text:
• Effectively-once: idemKey + idempotent projection updates.
  • Out-of-order: define event precedence per leg; recompute status from “facts” (dep/arr times).
  • Backfills: separate topic; projector is deterministic & replayable.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text:
• Partition by shipment_id (hash) across Kafka & DB. Cache “hot shipments”.
  • TTL old events → cold storage; compress JSON payloads.
  • Multi‑region: active/active Kafka + DB with regional keys; read local, write dual.

docs.title: Failure Modes
docs.text:
• Duplicate events → ignored by idemKey.
  • Poison messages → DLQ with alert.
  • Projection conflict → retry with exponential backoff.

docs.title: Security/PII
docs.text:
• JWT + tenant scoping; shipment_id ACLs; audit read access.
  • Minimize PII in payload; encryption at rest; WORM logging for compliance.

docs.title: Talk Track Bullets
docs.text:
• Lead with CQRS + event sourcing advantages (auditability, replay).
  • Emphasize idempotency and out‑of‑order handling.
  • Call out hot/cold storage and cache invalidation on ingest.

docs.title: Interview Structure Overview
docs.text:
• Round 1: Online Assessment / Initial Technical Screening: 1-2 coding problems on a platform like CoderPad, focusing on core data structures and their efficient implementation.
  • Round 2: Technical / Data Structures & Algorithms Round: A deep-dive 60-minute round with a focus on DSA, problem-solving, and often a concurrency element.
  • Round 3: System Design Round: A 60-minute round assessing your ability to design scalable, distributed systems. The focus is on trade-offs, component design, and communication.
  • Round 4: Hiring Manager / Behavioral Round: Evaluates project experience, leadership potential, cultural fit, and your motivation for joining Rubrik.

docs.title: Data Structures & Algorithms (Coding Rounds)
docs.text:
These problems test your core problem-solving skills. They range from medium to hard difficulty.

Arrays & Strings

  1. Container With Most Water Tests two-pointer technique.
  2. 3Sum Classic problem for handling duplicates with two-pointers.
  3. Product of Array Except Self Requires clever use of prefix/postfix products without division.
  4. Subarray Sum Equals K Excellent hash map problem involving prefix sums.
  5. Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters Classic sliding window problem.
  6. Minimum Window Substring Advanced sliding window problem.
  7. Rotate Image Tests in-place matrix manipulation.
  8. Valid Palindrome Good warm-up for string manipulation and two-pointers.

Linked Lists

  1. LRU Cache (High Priority) A very common question at Rubrik. Tests combined use of HashMap and Doubly Linked List for O(1) operations.
  2. Merge K Sorted Lists Classic problem solved efficiently with a Min-Heap.
  3. Reverse Nodes in k-Group Tests complex pointer manipulation.
  4. Copy List with Random Pointer Requires careful handling of pointers and a map to avoid cycles.

Trees & Graphs

  1. Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree (High Priority) Frequently asked. Tests tree traversal (DFS/BFS) and string manipulation.
  2. Binary Tree Level Order Traversal Fundamental BFS problem.
  3. Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree Classic recursion problem.
  4. Validate Binary Search Tree Tests understanding of BST properties.
  5. Kth Smallest Element in a BST Efficiently solved with in-order traversal.
  6. Number of Islands Fundamental graph traversal (DFS/BFS) on a grid.
  7. Clone Graph Tests graph traversal and use of a map to handle visited nodes.
  8. Course Schedule Classic topological sort problem to detect cycles in a graph.
  9. Word Ladder A great problem for finding the shortest path using BFS.

Heaps (Priority Queues)

  1. Find Median from Data Stream Classic problem using two heaps (Min-Heap and Max-Heap).
  2. Top K Frequent Elements Solved efficiently with a HashMap and a Min-Heap.
  3. Meeting Rooms II Interval problem that can be solved elegantly with a Min-Heap.

Dynamic Programming & Backtracking

  1. Coin Change Fundamental bottom-up DP problem.
  2. Longest Palindromic Substring Classic DP problem.
  3. Combination Sum A great introduction to backtracking.
  4. Letter Combinations of a Phone Number Another classic backtracking problem.

docs.title: Concurrency / Multithreading
docs.text:
Rubrik emphasizes strong concurrency fundamentals. You must be able to write thread-safe code.

  1. Print in Order A simple introduction to thread synchronization using locks or semaphores.
  2. Print FooBar Alternately Slightly more complex synchronization between two threads.
  3. The Dining Philosophers Problem Classic concurrency problem to prevent deadlock.
  4. Web Crawler Multithreaded Practical application of multithreading, requiring a shared data structure for visited links and URLs to crawl.
  5. Design a Thread-Safe Blocking Queue A fundamental concept often asked to be implemented from scratch.

docs.title: System Design Case Studies
docs.text:
For system design, there's no single "problem link." The goal is to discuss trade-offs. These links lead to detailed primers or case studies.

  1. Design a Rate Limiter (High Priority) Crucial for any distributed system. Understand algorithms like Token Bucket and Leaky Bucket.
  2. Design a URL Shortening Service (like TinyURL) Covers hash generation, scalability, and handling redirects.
  3. Design a Photo Sharing Service (like Instagram) Focus on feed generation, image storage (S3), and use of CDNs.
  4. Design a Distributed Job Scheduler (like cron) Focus on reliability, fault tolerance, and avoiding single points of failure.
  5. Design a Distributed Cache (like Redis/Memcached) Discuss sharding, replication, consistency, and eviction policies.
  6. Design a Leaderboard System Focus on data structures for fast updates and retrieval (e.g., Sorted Sets in Redis).
  7. Design a Typeahead Suggestion Service Discuss Trie-based data structures, ranking, and updating the suggestions.

docs.title: Rubrik‑Themed DSA Pack (30 Problems) — Senior Software Engineer (India)
docs.text: Each problem is inspired by Rubrik’s domain (backup, snapshots, dedupe, restores, policy engines, distributed storage). For every item: problem ➜ constraints ➜ approach ➜ complexity ➜ key edge cases. Code snippets are Python‑ish pseudocode unless noted.

docs.title: 1) Snapshot Interval Merge (Policy Compliance)
docs.text:
Problem. Given N snapshots each with [start, end] retention windows, merge overlaps and return total retained time and the merged intervals. Constraints. 1 ≤ N ≤ 1e5; intervals within 64‑bit time; return sorted non‑overlapping intervals. Approach. Sort by start; sweep merging by extending the current end if overlapping; accumulate duration. Complexity. O(N log N) time, O(N) space. Edge cases. Touching intervals [a,b] & [b,c] should merge if policy says “inclusive end”; empty durations. 

def merge_intervals(A):
    A.sort()
    out=[]; cur=None
    for s,e in A:
        if not cur or s>cur[1]:
            if cur: out.append(cur)
            cur=[s,e]
        else:
            cur[1]=max(cur[1],e)
    if cur: out.append(cur)
    total=sum(e-s for s,e in out)
    return out,total

docs.title: 2) Incremental Backup Planner (Min Deltas)
docs.text: Problem. Given daily changed‑byte counts C[i] and a weekly full backup cost F, choose which days to take full vs incremental to minimize total cost over M days; incremental on day i costs C[i]. Full resets incremental accumulation. Approach. DP: dp[i]=min(F+dp[i+1], C[i]+dp[i+1]) but with a constraint “at least one full per 7 days”. Use DP with windowed constraint or monotone deque. Complexity. O(M) time, O(M) space (can optimize to O(1)). Edge cases. Start/end of week boundaries; zero‑change days.

docs.title: 3) Multi‑Tenant Quota Enforcement (Sliding Window)
docs.text: Problem. For per‑tenant write requests (tenantId, t) enforce quota ≤ K requests in any sliding window of W seconds; return allow/deny stream. Approach. HashMap tenant→deque of timestamps; pop while t - deque[0] >= W; allow if len< K. Complexity. Amortized O(1)/request. Edge cases. Large tenant fan‑out; clock skew; exactly‑W boundary.

docs.title: 4) Dedup Index: First Duplicate Chunk
docs.text: Problem. Stream of chunk hashes H[ ] (64‑bit). Find the first index that repeats a previously seen hash. Approach. HashSet; return earliest index that appears twice, or −1. For memory constraints, use Bloom + second‑pass verify. Complexity. O(N) time, O(N) space. Edge cases. Collisions if using 32‑bit; can mention double‑hashing.

docs.title: 5) Restore Window Coverage (Minimum Tapes)
docs.text: Problem. You have tapes each covering a set of time intervals for a dataset. Choose minimum number of tapes whose union covers a requested window [L,R]. Approach. Greedy interval covering: sort by start; extend farthest end while start ≤ current_end. Complexity. O(N log N). Edge cases. Gaps (impossible restore), multiple optimal choices.

docs.title: 6) Immutable Log Compaction
docs.text: Problem. Given append‑only log segments with key,value,ts, compact to newest value per key while preserving order by ts for ties. Return compacted sequence. Approach. Process from newest to oldest tracking seenKeys; output when first time encountered; reverse at end. Complexity. O(N). Edge cases. Multiple updates same ts; tombstones.

docs.title: 7) Snapshot Dependency Graph (Topological Restore)
docs.text: Problem. Snapshots form a DAG (incrementals depend on previous). Given a target snapshot node, return restore order. Approach. Reverse topological order from target: DFS to collect ancestors, then topologically sort subgraph or do post‑order and reverse. Complexity. O(V+E). Edge cases. Multiple parents (multi‑base); cycles invalid — detect.

docs.title: 8) Consistent Hash Ring Rebalance
docs.text: Problem. Given N nodes on a consistent hash ring and M virtual nodes each, compute movement percentage of keys when adding one node. Approach. In a perfect hash, expected movement ≈ 1/(N+1); programmatically simulate: sort points, compute intervals absorbed by new node points. Complexity. O((N·M) log (N·M)). Edge cases. Non‑uniform vnode distribution.

docs.title: 9) Throttle Restore Streams (Token Bucket)
docs.text: Problem. Implement per‑job token bucket: requests of size s must acquire s tokens; tokens refill at rate R/sec up to burst B. Approach. Track tokens and lastRefillTs; on request, refill then check tokens>=s. Complexity. O(1). Edge cases. Large bursts; float precision; time reversal.

docs.title: 10) Tiering to Cold Storage (Knapsack Variant)
docs.text: Problem. Select files to move to cold storage so that freed hot‑tier size ≥ S while minimizing “future expected read cost” value. Each file i has size si and future read penalty pi. Approach. 0/1 knapsack by capacity S (minimize penalty while size≥S). Convert to maximize negative penalty; or DP by total size. Complexity. O(N·S) pseudo‑poly; for big S use greedy on ratio or meet‑in‑the‑middle. Edge cases. Exact S not possible, choose ≥ S minimal penalty.

docs.title: 11) Windowed Change‑Rate Anomaly (Prefix/Suffix)
docs.text: Problem. Given bytesWritten[i], mark indices where 7‑day average deviates > T× from 28‑day baseline. Approach. Prefix sums for O(1) window averages; compare ratios. Complexity. O(N). Edge cases. Division by zero baseline; leading windows.

docs.title: 12) File‑System Tree Compression (Run‑Length Path)
docs.text: Problem. Compress repetitive directory paths (e.g., a/a/a/a/b) into (segment, count) form; support decompress. Approach. Split by '/', run‑length encode contiguous equal segments. Complexity. O(L). Edge cases. Empty segments, root handling.

docs.title: 13) Change‑Set Diff (Minimal Operations)
docs.text: Problem. Two ordered lists of chunk IDs A and B; compute minimal edits (insert/delete/retain) to transform A→B. Approach. Classic edit distance with backtracking, or LCS to derive edits (keep on LCS, delete otherwise, insert for extras in B). Complexity. O(nm) DP; for large use Hunt‑Szymanski or Myers O((n+m)D). Edge cases. Duplicates; memory.

docs.title: 14) Backup Schedule Generator (Cron Simplifier)
docs.text: Problem. Given constraints: daily at HH:MM, weekly on D at HH:MM, skip holidays list — generate next K fire times. Approach. Iterate forward using min‑heap of rule candidates; skip if date in holidays. Complexity. O(K log R). Edge cases. DST transitions; leap years.

docs.title: 15) Snapshot Space Forecast (Exponential Smoothing)
docs.text: Problem. Forecast next 30‑day storage usage from daily totals. Approach. Single exponential smoothing or moving average; implement ES with alpha. Complexity. O(N). Edge cases. Cold starts, abrupt jumps.

docs.title: 16) Data‑Shard Repair (BFS on Erasure Groups)
docs.text: Problem. Erasure coding groups G with nodes; some nodes down. Find minimal set of remaining nodes to reconstruct a shard. Approach. For each group, if k of n available, choose any k (greedy). If cross‑group parity exists, model as bipartite selection and run BFS/DFS to find feasible picks. Complexity. O(E) for simple k‑of‑n; NP‑hard variants if cross‑deps complex. Edge cases. Multiple optimal; tie‑break by load.

docs.title: 17) Point‑in‑Time Restore (Binary Search)
docs.text: Problem. Given sorted snapshot timestamps and a target time T, find snapshot ≤ T that minimizes T−snapshot. Approach. Binary search lower_bound. Complexity. O(log N). Edge cases. Before first; after last.

docs.title: 18) Parallel Restore Planner (Top‑K Disjoint Files)
docs.text: Problem. For M files with sizes and conflict sets (can’t restore two conflicting simultaneously due to device contention), pick batches to maximize bytes/sec. Approach. Greedy with max‑heap on size filtering by conflicts; or reduce to maximum weighted independent set on interval/resource graph (heuristic). Complexity. Heuristic O(M log M). Edge cases. Many conflicts => small batches.

docs.title: 19) Chunk Coalescing (Monotonic Stack)
docs.text: Problem. Given chunk sizes along a stream, coalesce adjacent chunks if combined size ≤ L, maximizing number of merges. Return final partition. Approach. Stack of segments; try to merge top with incoming while total ≤ L. Complexity. O(N). Edge cases. Large single chunk; exact equality.

docs.title: 20) Policy Engine — First Match Wins
docs.text: Problem. Rules R[i] with predicates on (tenant, path, tag). For requests, return the first matching rule’s action. Rules can be added dynamically. Approach. Build trie on path + hash on tenant + bitsets for tags; evaluation orders: tenant → path → tag. Maintain rule order per bucket. Complexity. O(L + log B). Edge cases. Shadowed rules; rule deletion.

docs.title: 21) Audit Log Sampling (Reservoir)
docs.text: Problem. Stream of audit events; keep a uniform sample of size K over unbounded stream. Approach. Reservoir sampling (Vitter’s algorithm). Complexity. O(N) time, O(K) space. Edge cases. K≥N → keep all.

docs.title: 22) Version Graph Garbage Collection
docs.text: Problem. Directed acyclic version graph; given a set of pinned versions, delete minimal number of unpinned nodes that are not on any path from a root to a pinned node. Return deletable nodes. Approach. Mark phase: reverse‑reachability from pinned; sweep: delete unmarked. Complexity. O(V+E). Edge cases. Multiple roots; large fan‑out.

docs.title: 23) Distributed Lease Renewal (Heartbeats)
docs.text: Problem. Track N jobs sending heartbeats; detect expirations after T seconds of silence and return expired job IDs periodically. Approach. Min‑heap keyed by nextExpiry; map job→heapIndex; on heartbeat, update expiry and heapify. Complexity. O(log N) per heartbeat. Edge cases. Duplicate heartbeats; clock skew; spurious time jumps.

docs.title: 24) Restore Consistency Checker (Union‑Find)
docs.text: Problem. N files with constraints “file a must be restored before b” and “a conflicts with b (cannot co‑exist)”. Determine if constraints are satisfiable. Approach. Toposort for order constraints; conflict constraints → 2‑SAT/Union‑Find on components with parity if expressing mutual exclusion; or detect if any cycle or co‑location contradiction. Complexity. O(V+E). Edge cases. Self‑conflict; duplicate constraints.

docs.title: 25) Hotset Cache — LFU with Aging
docs.text: Problem. Implement LFU cache with periodic aging (halve counts every T). Supports get/put. Approach. Standard LFU (freq→DLL buckets), plus background “aging” to avoid stale heavy hitters. Complexity. O(1) amortized per op. Edge cases. Ties by recency; size 0.

docs.title: 26) Cloud Snapshot Pricing (Binary Search on Answer)
docs.text: Problem. Given per‑GB price tiers and a budget B, find maximum data X that can be stored without exceeding B. Approach. Binary search X; cost(X) via prefix of tiers. Complexity. O(log Range). Edge cases. Non‑contiguous tiers; off‑by‑one at boundaries.

docs.title: 27) Immutable Map with Snapshots (Persistent DS)
docs.text: Problem. Implement a versioned map supporting put(key,val) returning new version ID, and get(key, versionId). Approach. Persistent balanced BST or Hash‑array‑mapped trie (HAMT) with structural sharing. Complexity. O(log N) per op. Edge cases. Memory blowup without sharing; tombstones.

docs.title: 28) Tape Robot Scheduler (Intervals + Heap)
docs.text: Problem. Given tape mount requests (start, duration) and one robot arm, schedule to minimize late mounts. Approach. Sort by start; use min‑heap by finish; simulate; or use EDF with preemption if allowed. Complexity. O(N log N). Edge cases. Overlapping long jobs; preemption policy.

docs.title: 29) Multi‑Region Restore Latency (Min‑Cut Insight)
docs.text: Problem. Regions graph with bandwidth capacities. For requested data size S from region A to B, find minimal completion time if flows can use multiple paths. Approach. Max‑flow on capacity graph; time ≈ S / maxflow. Return maxflow and suggested path split. Complexity. O(E·sqrt(V)) or Dinic O(EV). Edge cases. Disconnected; per‑edge latency not considered (note extension to min‑cost flow).

docs.title: 30) Alert Flood Deduplication (Time Buckets)
docs.text: Problem. Collapse identical alerts arriving within Δ seconds into one with count. Return collapsed stream. Approach. HashMap key→(lastTs,count); if ts - lastTs ≤ Δ, increment count; else emit new. Complexity. O(N). Edge cases. Out‑of‑order alerts; window stitch across boundaries.

docs.title: Appendix: Quick Patterns & Why They Fit Rubrik
docs.text:
• Intervals & sweeps for retention & restore windows.
  • Graphs/Topo/Flow for snapshot DAGs, dependency orders, and multi‑region bandwidth.
  • Heaps & deques for schedulers, sliding windows.
  • Union‑Find/2‑SAT for constraint satisfiability.
  • Persistent DS models immutable snapshots.
  • Binary search on answer for cost/latency caps.
  • Streaming (reservoir, token bucket) for audit/throttle.

docs.title: Two Coding Problems — Explanations, Optimized Approaches, and C++ Code
docs.text: This document summarizes two interview-style problems shown in the screenshots, with clear problem statements, optimized approaches, and ready-to-run C++ implementations (plus small tests).

docs.title: Problem 1 — Sliding Blocks Exit to the Right
Restated Problem
docs.text:
You’re given a grid (height × width). Each cell is: - . empty - x wall (top row, bottom row, and first column) - 0..9 a block id (same id forms a single connected piece, possibly covering multiple cells/rows)

When you choose a block id, that block slides only to the right until it either exits the grid or collides with another block. At each turn you must output one block id to move; the judge applies the move and re-calls your function with the new grid. A valid solution/ordering is guaranteed to exist.

Task (per turn): Return an id that can be safely removed now (i.e., sliding right won’t hit anything). If multiple are possible, any valid one works (we pick the smallest id for determinism).

Constraints: width, height ≤ 15, nb_blocks ≤ 10.

docs.title: Approach A (O(H·W)) — Right-to-left row sweep to build blockers
docs.text:
Key observation: A block A is removable now iff in every row it occupies, there is no other block to its right before the edge.

We can compute all “blockers” in one pass per row: - Sweep a row right-to-left, keeping nearest = the nearest block id to the right seen so far. - When we meet a cell with block B, the current nearest (if any and different) is the unique blocker in this row, meaning B cannot exit before nearest leaves. - Aggregate blockers across rows → a small DAG between ids. Any id with indegree = 0 is safe to move now.

This is linear in the grid size: O(height × width) per turn.

docs.title: C++ (no comments)
docs.text:
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int solve(int width, int height, int nb_blocks, const vector<string>& g) {
    const int B=10;
    bool present[B]={0};
    bool edge[B][B]{}; 
    for (int r=0;r<height;++r){
        int nearest=-1;
        for (int c=width-1;c>=0;--c){
            char ch=g[r][c];
            if (ch>='0'&&ch<='9'){
                int b=ch-'0';
                present[b]=true;
                if (nearest!=-1 && nearest!=b) edge[nearest][b]=true;
                nearest=b;
            }
        }
    }
    int indeg[B]={0};
    bool any=false;
    for (int u=0;u<nb_blocks;++u) if (present[u]) {
        any=true;
        for (int v=0;v<nb_blocks;++v) if (edge[v][u]) ++indeg[u];
    }
    if (!any) return 0;
    for (int b=0;b<nb_blocks;++b) if (present[b] && indeg[b]==0) return b;
    for (int b=0;b<nb_blocks;++b) if (present[b]) return b;
    return 0;
}

docs.title: Approach B (O(H·W) but more explicit) — Per-block rightmost + first obstacle
docs.text:
1. For each block b and each row r, record the rightmost column that b occupies (rightmost[b][r]).
  2. From that column, scan right to find the first block; if some block k is encountered, mark k blocks b.
  3. Choose any id with indegree 0 (we return the smallest such id).

docs.title: C++ (no comments)
docs.text:
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int solve(int width, int height, int nb_blocks, const vector<string>& grid) {
    const int MAXB = 10;
    vector<bool> present(MAXB, false);
    vector<array<int, 32>> rightmost(MAXB);
    for (int b = 0; b < MAXB; ++b) rightmost[b].fill(-1);
    for (int r = 0; r < height; ++r) {
        for (int c = 0; c < width; ++c) {
            char ch = grid[r][c];
            if (ch >= '0' && ch <= '9') {
                int b = ch - '0';
                present[b] = true;
                rightmost[b][r] = max(rightmost[b][r], c);
            }
        }
    }
    array<int, MAXB> indeg{};
    indeg.fill(0);
    bool blocksExist = false;
    for (int b = 0; b < nb_blocks; ++b) {
        if (!present[b]) continue;
        blocksExist = true;
        unordered_set<int> blockers;
        for (int r = 0; r < height; ++r) {
            int c0 = rightmost[b][r];
            if (c0 == -1) continue;
            for (int c = c0 + 1; c < width; ++c) {
                char ch = grid[r][c];
                if (ch >= '0' && ch <= '9') {
                    int k = ch - '0';
                    if (k != b) blockers.insert(k);
                    break;
                }
            }
        }
        indeg[b] = (int)blockers.size();
    }
    if (!blocksExist) return 0;
    for (int b = 0; b < nb_blocks; ++b)
        if (present[b] && indeg[b] == 0)
            return b;
    for (int b = 0; b < nb_blocks; ++b)
        if (present[b]) return b;
    return 0;
}

docs.title: Problem 2 — Count 4-Shop Paths (One of Each Type)
Restated Problem
docs.text:
You have an undirected graph of shops. shops[i] ∈ {0,1,2,3} is the type of node i (bookshop, school shop, sport store, stationery). Roads are undirected edges.

Task: Count the number of ordered simple paths of length 3 edges (4 nodes) that visit exactly one shop of each type (types all distinct, order can be any). Visiting the same 4 nodes in different orders counts as different paths. Constraints: N ≤ 50, E ≤ 250.

docs.title: Approach A — Bitmask DP over types (classic)
docs.text:
Let dp[mask][v] be the number of paths ending at node v with exactly the set of types mask used, where mask includes type(v).

Initialization: dp[1<<type(v)][v] = 1 for all v. Transition: for an edge v→u, if type(u) not in mask, then dp[mask | (1<<type(u))][u] += dp[mask][v]. Answer is sum_v dp[1111][v].

docs.title: C++ (no comments)
docs.text:
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

long long countPathsDP(const vector<int>& shops, const vector<vector<int>>& roads) {
    int n = shops.size();
    vector<vector<int>> adj(n);
    for (auto &e : roads) { int a=e[0], b=e[1]; adj[a].push_back(b); adj[b].push_back(a); }
    const int FULL = 15;
    vector<vector<long long>> dp(16, vector<long long>(n, 0));
    for (int v=0; v<n; ++v) dp[1<<shops[v]][v] = 1;
    for (int mask=1; mask<=FULL; ++mask) {
        for (int v=0; v<n; ++v) if (dp[mask][v]) {
            for (int u: adj[v]) {
                int bit = 1 << shops[u];
                if ((mask & bit) == 0) dp[mask | bit][u] += dp[mask][v];
            }
        }
    }
    long long ans = 0;
    for (int v=0; v<n; ++v) ans += dp[FULL][v];
    return ans;
}

docs.title: Approach B — Meet-in-the-middle on the middle edge (near-linear in E)
docs.text:
Every valid 4-node ordered path a – u – v – d has a middle directed edge (u→v) and four distinct types {type(a), type(u), type(v), type(d)}.

Precompute, for each node, the count of neighbors by type. For each directed edge u→v with type(u)≠type(v), choose: - a from neighbors of u with a type ta ∉ {type(u), type(v)}, - d from neighbors of v with a type td ∉ {type(u), type(v), ta}.

Sum cnt[u][ta] * cnt[v][td] over all ta, td that satisfy the distinctness constraints. This counts each ordered 4-node path exactly once per orientation. Complexity: O(E × 16) with tiny constants.

docs.title: C++ (no comments)
docs.text:
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

long long countPathsEdge(const vector<int>& shops, const vector<vector<int>>& roads) {
    int n=shops.size();
    vector<vector<int>> adj(n);
    for (auto &e:roads){int a=e[0],b=e[1]; adj[a].push_back(b); adj[b].push_back(a);}
    vector<array<int,4>> cnt(n);
    for (int u=0;u<n;++u){
        cnt[u]={0,0,0,0};
        for (int v:adj[u]) ++cnt[u][shops[v]];
    }
    long long ans=0;
    for (int u=0;u<n;++u){
        for (int v:adj[u]){
            int tu=shops[u], tv=shops[v];
            if (tu==tv) continue;
            for (int ta=0;ta<4;++ta) if (ta!=tu && ta!=tv){
                for (int td=0;td<4;++td) if (td!=tu && td!=tv && td!=ta){
                    ans += 1LL*cnt[u][ta]*cnt[v][td];
                }
            }
        }
    }
    return ans;
}

docs.text: Problem 1 is interactive—your solve(...) is called each turn with the current grid; you output a single id each time. The code above returns a safe id at that turn. You can still unit-test by crafting static grids and verifying the returned id is among valid zero-indegree choices.

docs.title: When to Use Which
docs.text:
• Problem 1: Prefer the row sweep blocker build (Approach A). It’s linear, branch-predictable, and simple.
  • Problem 2: Prefer the edge-center solution for raw speed and minimal memory. Use bitmask DP if you later generalize to more than four types or different path lengths.

docs.title: Two Sum
docs.text:
ID: two-sum Difficulty: Easy Tags: Array, Hash Table Pattern: Hashing, Single Pass

Given an integer array nums and an integer target, return the indices of the two numbers such that they add up to target.

Assumptions: - Exactly one valid pair exists. - You may not reuse the same element. - Order of indices doesn't matter (return either (i, j) or (j, i)).

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text: We need two values a and b where a + b = target. For each element we can check if the complement target - nums[i] was seen earlier. A hash map from value -> index lets us do this in O(1) average time per element.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text: Traverse once, store numbers as you go. For each number, look up its needed complement.

docs.title: Correctness Argument
docs.text: When at index i, all indices < i are already stored. If the complement exists among them we immediately return the pair. Because exactly one solution exists, we will encounter the first finishing index where its complement already appeared.

docs.title: Edge Cases
docs.text:
• Minimum length array (size 2) works directly.
  • Duplicate numbers (e.g. [3,3], target 6) handled since first 3 stored then second finds it.
  • Negative numbers: hash map unaffected.

docs.title: Implementations
Complexity
docs.text: Approach Time Space Notes Single-pass hash map O(n) O(n) Each element stored at most once

docs.title: Follow Ups
docs.text:
1. Return the actual values instead of indices.
  2. If multiple pairs exist, collect all (requires storing lists of indices per value).
  3. Streaming variant: maintain map as numbers arrive, emit pair when found.

docs.title: Test Yourself
docs.text: Try a quick dry run: nums = [2,7,11,15], target=9 -> complement 7 found when i=1. Edge duplicate: nums = [3,2,4], target=6 -> store 3,2 then complement 2 found at index 2 producing (1,2). Duplicate pair: nums = [3,3], target=6 -> second 3 finds first.

docs.title: Backend SDE-1 Project Ideas 🚀
docs.text: Here’s a curated list of backend projects perfect for SDE-1 level, with concise implementation details, tech stacks, and learning outcomes. Each project is designed to highlight core backend concepts like APIs, concurrency, authentication, and distributed systems.

docs.title: 1. 🌐 URL Shortener with Analytics
docs.text:
Overview: Build a service that converts long URLs into short, shareable links. Track every visit for analytics.

Core Features: - Generate unique short links (Base62/hash) - Redirect short links to original URLs - Track visits: IP, user-agent, timestamp - Analytics dashboard (clicks, devices, geo) - API endpoints for CRUD operations

Tech Stack: FastAPI / Flask, Redis, PostgreSQL

Learning Outcomes: - REST API design - Database schema for mapping and analytics - Caching with Redis - Security: rate limiting, input validation

Possible Extensions: - Custom aliases for short links - Expiry for links - QR code generation

docs.title: 2. 🔐 Auth-as-a-Service (JWT + OAuth2)
docs.text:
Overview: A plug-and-play authentication backend supporting email/password and OAuth2 (Google) login.

Core Features: - Register/login with email/password (bcrypt) - Google OAuth2 login - JWT access/refresh tokens - Token revocation (Redis) - Role-based access control (RBAC) - Middleware for protected routes

Tech Stack: Node.js / FastAPI, PostgreSQL, Redis

Learning Outcomes: - Secure password storage - OAuth2 flow - Stateless authentication with JWT - Session invalidation

Possible Extensions: - Email verification - Password reset - Multi-factor authentication

docs.title: 3. ⚙️ Job Queue System (Celery Lite)
docs.text:
Overview: A lightweight background job system to offload long-running tasks from the main app.

Core Features: - API to enqueue jobs - Redis-backed queue - Worker pool (multiprocessing/asyncio) - Track job status: pending, running, done, failed - Web dashboard for job monitoring

Tech Stack: Python, Redis, multiprocessing/asyncio

Learning Outcomes: - Producer-consumer pattern - Task serialization/deserialization - Worker orchestration - Real-time status updates

Possible Extensions: - Retry failed jobs - Scheduled jobs (cron) - Priority queues

docs.title: Binary Search on Answer Pattern
docs.text:
Define search space [lo, hi]; while lo < hi: mid; if feasible(mid) hi=mid else lo=mid+1.

long long minimizeMax(vector<int>& a, int k){
    sort(a.begin(), a.end());
    auto can = [&](int x){
        int pairs=0; for(int i=1;i<a.size();++i){ if(a[i]-a[i-1] <= x){ pairs++; i++; } }
        return pairs >= k;
    };
    int lo=0, hi=a.back()-a.front();
    while(lo<hi){
        int mid = lo + (hi-lo)/2;
        if(can(mid)) hi=mid; else lo=mid+1;
    }
    return lo;
}

docs.title: Ternary Search (Double Peak Avoided)
docs.text:
double ternarySearch(function<double(double)> f, double l, double r){
    for(int it=0; it<200; ++it){
        double m1 = l + (r-l)/3.0;
        double m2 = r - (r-l)/3.0;
        if(f(m1) < f(m2)) l = m1; else r = m2; // for maximum invert condition
    }
    return (l+r)/2.0;
}

docs.title: 1. Sliding Window
docs.text:
• Find subarrays or substrings that match certain properties.
  • Problems: Maximum/Minimum subarray sum, longest substring without repeating characters.
int maxSumSubarray(vector<int>& nums, int k) {
    int n       = nums.size();
    int max_sum = 0;
    int curr    = 0;

    for (int i = 0; i < k; ++i) {
        curr += nums[i];
    }
    max_sum = curr;

    for (int i = k; i < n; ++i) {
        curr += nums[i] - nums[i - k];
        max_sum = max(max_sum, curr);
    }
    return max_sum;
}

docs.title: 2. Two Pointers
docs.text:
• Used for searching pairs/triplets, reversing, or partitioning.
  • Problems: Pair sum, move zeroes, reverse array in-place.
vector<int> twoSumSorted(vector<int>& nums, int target) {
    int left  = 0;
    int right = (int)nums.size() - 1;

    while (left < right) {
        int sum = nums[left] + nums[right];
        if (sum == target) return { left, right };
        if (sum < target)  ++left; else --right;
    }
    return {};
}

docs.title: 5. Binary Search
docs.text:
• For searching in sorted arrays, or to answer "minimum/maximum" problems (search space).
  • Problems: Find element, first/last occurrence, search insert position.

int binarySearch(const vector<int>& nums, int target) {
    int left  = 0;
    int right = (int)nums.size() - 1;
    while (left <= right) {
        int mid = left + (right - left) / 2;
        if (nums[mid] == target) return mid;
        if (nums[mid] < target)  left = mid + 1; else right = mid - 1;
    }
    return -1;
}

// Reverse in-place (two-pointer)
void reverse(vector<int>& arr) {
    int l = 0;
    int r = (int)arr.size() - 1;
    while (l < r) {
        swap(arr[l++], arr[r--]);
    }
}

// Rotate right by k (three reversals)
void rotate(vector<int>& arr, int k) {
    int n = (int)arr.size();
    if (n == 0) return;
    k %= n;
    std::reverse(arr.begin(), arr.end());
    std::reverse(arr.begin(), arr.begin() + k);
    std::reverse(arr.begin() + k, arr.end());
}

docs.title: ⚠️ Common Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Off‑by‑one errors with left <= right vs left < right in binary search.
  • Forgetting to handle empty input (n == 0) before accessing nums[0].
  • Using extra arrays when in‑place two‑pointer solution exists (space waste).
  • Not normalizing rotation (k %= n).
  • Overflow when summing large values (use 64-bit / long long).

docs.title: Dynamic Programming
docs.text: Dynamic Programming (DP) breaks problems into overlapping subproblems with optimal substructure, caching solutions to avoid recomputation.

docs.title: At a Glance
docs.text:
Dimension Typical Complexity Example 1D O(n) Fibonacci, Climb Stairs 2D O(n*m) Edit Distance, Grid Paths Knapsack O(n*W) 0/1 Knapsack Bitmask O(n * 2^n) Traveling Salesman subset DP Digit DP O(pos * tight * state) Count numbers with property Tree DP O(n) Diameter, Independent Set

docs.title: Key Concepts
docs.text:
• Optimal substructure, overlapping subproblems
  • Top-down (memoization) vs bottom-up (tabulation)
  • State definition: parameters fully describe subproblem
  • Transitions: relation combining smaller sub-solutions
  • Base cases: smallest solvable units
  • Order of evaluation ensuring dependencies solved first
  • Space optimization via dropping obsolete dimensions

// Top-down
long long fib(int n, vector<long long>& dp){
    if(n<=1) return n;
    if(dp[n]!=-1) return dp[n];
    return dp[n]=fib(n-1,dp)+fib(n-2,dp);
}

// Bottom-up
long long fibBU(int n){
    if(n<=1) return n; long long a=0,b=1;
    for(int i=2;i<=n;++i){ long long c=a+b; a=b; b=c; }
    return b;
}

docs.text:
int knap(vector<int>& wt, vector<int>& val, int W){
    vector<int> dp(W+1, 0);
    for(int i=0;i<wt.size();++i){
        for(int w=W; w>=wt[i]; --w){
            dp[w] = max(dp[w], val[i] + dp[w-wt[i]]);
        }
    }
    return dp[W];
}

int LIS(vector<int>& a){
    vector<int> tail;
    for(int x: a){
        auto it = lower_bound(tail.begin(), tail.end(), x);
        if(it==tail.end()) tail.push_back(x); else *it=x;
    }
    return tail.size();
}

docs.title: Edit Distance
docs.text:
int editDistance(const string& a, const string& b){
    int n=a.size(), m=b.size();
    vector<vector<int>> dp(n+1, vector<int>(m+1));
    for(int i=0;i<=n;++i) dp[i][0]=i;
    for(int j=0;j<=m;++j) dp[0][j]=j;
    for(int i=1;i<=n;++i){
        for(int j=1;j<=m;++j){
            if(a[i-1]==b[j-1]) dp[i][j]=dp[i-1][j-1];
            else dp[i][j]=1+min({dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1], dp[i-1][j-1]});
        }
    }
    return dp[n][m];
}

docs.title: Graphs
docs.text: Graphs consist of nodes (vertices) and edges. They model relationships and connections between entities and are fundamental in computer science for representing networks, maps, and more.

docs.title: 📖 Key Concepts
docs.text:
• Graph Types: directed / undirected, weighted / unweighted, cyclic / acyclic, DAG
  • Density: sparse (adjacency list) vs dense (matrix)
  • Traversal: BFS (level order, shortest unweighted) vs DFS (structure, cycles, components)
  • Shortest Paths: BFS (unweighted), Dijkstra (non-negative weights), Bellman-Ford (neg edges), Floyd-Warshall (all-pairs), 0-1 BFS (edges of weight 0/1), A* (heuristic)
  • Ordering: Topological sort (Kahn / DFS postorder) for DAGs
  • Connectivity: components, bridges, articulation points, strongly connected components (Kosaraju / Tarjan)
  • Trees vs Graphs: Trees are connected, acyclic, V = E + 1 (undirected)
  • Representation trade-offs: adjacency list (space), matrix (O(1) edge check), edge list (sorting/DSU)
  • Common Patterns: multi-source BFS, layering, coloring, DSU for connectivity/MST, heap for weighted shortest paths

    seen[start] = 1;
    while (!q.empty()) {
        int u = q.front(); q.pop();
        order.push_back(u);
        for (int v : adj[u]) if (!seen[v]) { seen[v] = 1; q.push(v); }
    }
    return order;
}

inline void dfsRec(int u, const AdjList& adj, std::vector<char>& seen, std::vector<int>& order) {
    seen[u] = 1;
    order.push_back(u);
    for (int v : adj[u]) if (!seen[v]) dfsRec(v, adj, seen, order);
}
inline std::vector<int> dfs(int start, const AdjList& adj) {
    std::vector<int> order; std::vector<char> seen(adj.size());
    dfsRec(start, adj, seen, order);
    return order;
}

inline std::vector<int> topo_kahn(const AdjList& adj) {
    int n = (int)adj.size();
    std::vector<int> indeg(n), order;
    for (int u = 0; u < n; ++u) for (int v : adj[u]) indeg[v]++;
    std::queue<int> q; for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) if (!indeg[i]) q.push(i);
    while (!q.empty()) {
        int u = q.front(); q.pop(); order.push_back(u);
        for (int v : adj[u]) if (--indeg[v] == 0) q.push(v);
    }
    if ((int)order.size() != n) return {};
    return order;
}

struct WeightedEdge { int to; int w; };
using WAdjList = std::vector<std::vector<WeightedEdge>>;

inline std::vector<long long> dijkstra(const WAdjList& g, int src) {
    const long long INF = (1LL<<60);
    int n = (int)g.size();
    std::vector<long long> dist(n, INF);
    dist[src] = 0;
    using P = std::pair<long long,int>;
    std::priority_queue<P, std::vector<P>, std::greater<P>> pq;
    pq.push({0, src});
    while (!pq.empty()) {
        auto [d,u] = pq.top(); pq.pop();
        if (d != dist[u]) continue;
        for (auto [v,w] : g[u]) {
            long long nd = d + w;
            if (nd < dist[v]) { dist[v] = nd; pq.push({nd, v}); }
        }
    }
    return dist;
}

inline void apDfs(int u, int parent, const AdjList& g, std::vector<int>& tin, std::vector<int>& low,
                  std::vector<char>& vis, int& timer, std::vector<char>& isAP) {
    vis[u] = 1; tin[u] = low[u] = ++timer; int children = 0;
    for (int v : g[u]) {
        if (v == parent) continue;
        if (!vis[v]) {
            ++children;
            apDfs(v, u, g, tin, low, vis, timer, isAP);
            low[u] = std::min(low[u], low[v]);
            if (parent != -1 && low[v] >= tin[u]) isAP[u] = 1;
        } else low[u] = std::min(low[u], tin[v]);
    }
    if (parent == -1 && children > 1) isAP[u] = 1;
}
inline std::vector<int> articulation_points(const AdjList& g) {
    int n = (int)g.size();
    std::vector<int> tin(n,-1), low(n,-1);
    std::vector<char> vis(n), isAP(n);
    int timer = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) if (!vis[i]) apDfs(i, -1, g, tin, low, vis, timer, isAP);
    std::vector<int> res; for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) if (isAP[i]) res.push_back(i);
    return res;
}

vector<int> dijkstra(int n, vector<vector<pair<int,int>>>& adj, int src) {
    const int INF = 1e9;

        if (d != dist[u]) continue; // stale entry
        for (auto [v, w] : adj[u]) {

                dist[v] = d + w;
                pq.push({dist[v], v});

    }

}

#pragma once
#include <bits/stdc++.h>

class LRUCache {
public:
    explicit LRUCache(int capacity) : cap_(capacity) {}

    int get(int key) {
        auto it = pos_.find(key);
        if (it == pos_.end()) return -1;
        touch(it);
        return it->second->second;
    }

    void put(int key, int value) {
        auto it = pos_.find(key);
        if (it != pos_.end()) {
            it->second->second = value;
            touch(it);
        } else {
            if ((int)list_.size() == cap_) {
                auto last = list_.back();
                pos_.erase(last.first);
                list_.pop_back();
            }
            list_.emplace_front(key, value);
            pos_[key] = list_.begin();
        }
    }

private:
    int cap_;
    std::list<std::pair<int,int>> list_;
    std::unordered_map<int, std::list<std::pair<int,int>>::iterator> pos_;

    void touch(std::unordered_map<int, std::list<std::pair<int,int>>::iterator>::iterator it) {
        list_.splice(list_.begin(), list_, it->second);
    }
};

// Max-heap of ints
template <class T>
class BinaryHeap {
    vector<T> a; // 0-index
public:
    bool empty() const { return a.empty(); }
    int size() const { return a.size(); }
    const T& top() const { return a[0]; }
    void push(const T& val){
        a.push_back(val);
        int i = a.size()-1;
        while(i>0){
            int p=(i-1)/2;
            if(a[p] >= a[i]) break;
            swap(a[p], a[i]);
            i=p;
        }
    }
    void pop(){
        swap(a[0], a.back());
        a.pop_back();
        int n=a.size(), i=0;
        while(true){
            int l=2*i+1, r=2*i+2, big=i;
            if(l<n && a[l] > a[big]) big=l;
            if(r<n && a[r] > a[big]) big=r;
            if(big==i) break;
            swap(a[i], a[big]);
            i=big;
        }
    }
};

class MedianFinder {
    priority_queue<int> lo; // max-heap
    priority_queue<int, vector<int>, greater<int>> hi; // min-heap
public:
    void addNum(int num){
        if(lo.empty() || num <= lo.top()) lo.push(num); else hi.push(num);
        // balance
        if(lo.size() > hi.size()+1){ hi.push(lo.top()); lo.pop(); }
        else if(hi.size() > lo.size()){ lo.push(hi.top()); hi.pop(); }
    }
    double findMedian(){
        if(lo.size()==hi.size()) return (lo.top()+hi.top())/2.0;
        return lo.top();
    }
};

ListNode* reverse(ListNode* head) {
    ListNode* prev = nullptr;
    while (head) {
        ListNode* nxt = head->next;
        head->next = prev;
        prev = head;
        head = nxt;
    }
    return prev;
}

bool hasCycle(ListNode* head) {
    ListNode *slow = head, *fast = head;
    while (fast && fast->next) {
        slow = slow->next;
        fast = fast->next->next;
        if (slow == fast) return true;
    }
    return false;
}

ListNode* detectCycle(ListNode* head) {
    ListNode *slow = head, *fast = head;
    while (fast && fast->next) {
        slow = slow->next; fast = fast->next->next;
        if (slow == fast) {
            slow = head;
            while (slow != fast) { slow = slow->next; fast = fast->next; }
            return slow; // entry
        }
    }
    return nullptr;
}

ListNode* removeNthFromEnd(ListNode* head, int n) {
    ListNode dummy(0);
    dummy.next = head;
    ListNode *first = &dummy, *second = &dummy;
    for (int i = 0; i < n + 1; ++i)
        first = first->next;
    while (first) {
        first = first->next;
        second = second->next;
    }
    second->next = second->next->next;
    return dummy.next;
}

ListNode* mergeTwoLists(ListNode* l1, ListNode* l2) {
    ListNode dummy(0);
    ListNode* tail = &dummy;
    while (l1 && l2) {
        if (l1->val < l2->val) {
            tail->next = l1;
            l1 = l1->next;
        } else {
            tail->next = l2;
            l2 = l2->next;
        }
        tail = tail->next;
    }
    tail->next = l1 ? l1 : l2;
    return dummy.next;
}

#pragma once
#include <bits/stdc++.h>

template <class T>
class Fenwick {
public:
    Fenwick() = default;
    explicit Fenwick(int n) { init(n); }
    explicit Fenwick(const std::vector<T>& a) { build(a); }

    void init(int n) {
        n_ = n;
        bit_.assign(n_ + 1, T{});
    }

    void build(const std::vector<T>& a) {
        init((int)a.size());
        for (int i = 0; i < n_; ++i) add(i, a[i]);
    }

    void add(int idx, T val) {
        for (int i = idx + 1; i <= n_; i += i & -i)
            bit_[i] = bit_[i] + val;
    }

    T prefix(int idx) const {
        T res{};
        for (int i = idx + 1; i > 0; i -= i & -i)
            res = res + bit_[i];
        return res;
    }

    T range(int l, int r) const {
        if (l > r) return T{};
        return prefix(r) - (l ? prefix(l - 1) : T{});
    }

    int size() const { return n_; }

    int kth(long long k) const {
        int idx = 0;
        int bitMask = 1 << (31 - __builtin_clz(n_));
        T cur{};
        for (int step = bitMask; step > 0; step >>= 1) {
            int nxt = idx + step;
            if (nxt <= n_ && cur + bit_[nxt] < k) {
                cur = cur + bit_[nxt];
                idx = nxt;
            }
        }
        return idx; // 0-based position where cumulative >= k is idx
    }

private:
    int n_ = 0;
    std::vector<T> bit_;
};

#pragma once
#include <bits/stdc++.h>

template <class T, class Op>
class SegmentTree {
public:
    SegmentTree() = default;
    explicit SegmentTree(const std::vector<T>& data) { build(data); }

    void build(const std::vector<T>& data) {
        n_ = (int)data.size();
        if (!n_) return;
        tree_.assign(4 * n_, Op::identity());
        buildRec(1, 0, n_ - 1, data);
    }

    void update(int idx, const T& val) { updateRec(1, 0, n_ - 1, idx, val); }

    T query(int l, int r) const {
        if (l > r) return Op::identity();
        l = std::max(l, 0);
        r = std::min(r, n_ - 1);
        return queryRec(1, 0, n_ - 1, l, r);
    }

    int size() const { return n_; }

private:
    int n_ = 0;
    std::vector<T> tree_;

    void buildRec(int p, int l, int r, const std::vector<T>& a) {
        if (l == r) {
            tree_[p] = a[l];
            return;
        }
        int m = (l + r) / 2;
        buildRec(p * 2, l, m, a);
        buildRec(p * 2 + 1, m + 1, r, a);
        tree_[p] = Op{}(tree_[p * 2], tree_[p * 2 + 1]);
    }

    void updateRec(int p, int l, int r, int idx, const T& val) {
        if (l == r) {
            tree_[p] = val;
            return;
        }
        int m = (l + r) / 2;
        if (idx <= m) updateRec(p * 2, l, m, idx, val); else updateRec(p * 2 + 1, m + 1, r, idx, val);
        tree_[p] = Op{}(tree_[p * 2], tree_[p * 2 + 1]);
    }

    T queryRec(int p, int l, int r, int ql, int qr) const {
        if (qr < l || r < ql) return Op::identity();
        if (ql <= l && r <= qr) return tree_[p];
        int m = (l + r) / 2;
        return Op{}(queryRec(p * 2, l, m, ql, qr), queryRec(p * 2 + 1, m + 1, r, ql, qr));
    }
};
